title: Council Post: 7 Marketing Trends To Watch In 2024 (And How To Put Them To Use)
text:
Jennifer Chase is Chief Marketing Officer and Executive Vice President at SAS.
The emergence of consumer-facing applications like ChatGPT was a wake-up call to the marketing department. If technology can generate never-ending episodes of Seinfeld, retroactively cast Bill Murray in The Lord of the Rings cinematic universe and write essays for university students, how could it not have an impact on a storyteller's discipline?
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) will continue to command center stage in the public imagination in 2024, but other trends will impact your marketing organization in 2024 as well. Let’s take a look at what I believe will be the most impactful marketing trends this year.
1. Generative AI
A well-governed GenAI approach has enormous upside for a marketing organization. IDC predicts that GenAI will take over 30% of marketing’s mundane tasks by 2027. This will free marketers to focus on higher-value tasks. Picture auto-generated email summaries of longer-form content or promos for videos and webinars created and formatted across media channels.
But marketers must also wrap their heads around using GenAI as more than a time- and cost-saver—it is a tool to drive customer experiences and engagement. Deep personalization of messaging, unscripted chat conversation and enhanced SEO are only a few examples of customer-focused rather than cost-focused applications.
The Association of National Advertisers features several resources on GenAI's strategic power, including this playbook.
2. Responsible AI
GenAI raises new ethical and legal considerations. There’s the thorny issue of intellectual property rights of creators whose work is used for training. GenAI’s accuracy is questionable—in fact, it will lie when prompted, making a human in the loop critical. These only compound existing concerns around the evergreen issue of data privacy, its susceptibility to bias and the suitability of underlying data pools.
GenAI has also attracted the attention of governments and regulators. In the U.S., there are several legislative and regulatory proposals on the table addressing AI. Other jurisdictions worldwide are considering or have already passed AI legislation, such as the EU.
Beyond legal compliance, the responsible use of AI must be an internally driven commitment to fairness, transparency and accountability, ensuring AI is implemented in a way that does no harm and avoids high-profile AI missteps that can cost organizations their reputation and customer loyalty.
3. Managing Talent
Almost two-thirds of marketers fear losing their jobs to AI in the next five years. However, I believe marketers should not fear AI taking their jobs—they should fear being edged out by fellow marketers who are more proficient in AI.
Like any technology, there's a learning curve involved. Support in the shape of training and data science education will be critical to your team's success. It's an investment in their futures as marketers and their professional development makes them more valuable to your team and organization.
The ANA and its Global CMO Growth Council have developed a talent resource, The 2023 Marketing Capabilities Framework, that provides marketing leaders with an industrywide playbook to elevate modern marketing talent.
4. Data Deprecation
The demise of the third-party cookie may seem like a challenge, but I see it as an opportunity to focus on more relevant and valuable data. Here’s a short version of what to do as you begin to rely more on your own data for a comprehensive customer profile:
Create a transparent value exchange.
Let customers know upfront what data you’re collecting, why you’re collecting it and what they get in exchange. Promise (and deliver) real-time offers that are relevant and valuable to them.
Build a complete customer identity.
Identity management and resolution can help ascertain whether the Robert J. Smith, Jim Smith and Bob Smith in your database are the same entity and even resolve anonymous guest interactions to the customer library. This can help provide a clearer picture of the customer.
Get a handle on second-party data.
Second-party data—collected, anonymized and monetized by other organizations—can help fill out your customer picture. And, of course, your own first-party data can be leveraged by other organizations for a price as well.
5. MarTech Sprawl
This is the year to reconcile the marketing stack, the data within it and its ecosystem interdependencies. Accept that decisions made a year ago might not make sense anymore, and look toward streamlining your current technology while optimizing its effectiveness. There's a payoff in operational costs, and license management tools can continue that efficiency going forward.
6. Analysts, Influencers And Peer Reviews
Industry analysts are the OG influencers, particularly in B2B markets. Their influence through vendor rating reports and buyer decision inquiries is still unmatched, even though the ability to influence has broadened tremendously in a creator economy where anyone can host a podcast, write a post and produce videos.
Increasingly, in a B2B context, peer reviews may eclipse both. More than 90% of B2B buyers told G2 they were more likely to purchase a product or service after reading a positive peer review. Use those AI skills to reach out to candidates for effective reviews and keep on top of social media and peer review sites to hear what customers are saying to leverage the voices that advocate for your brand.
7. Proving Your Worth
Market uncertainty is now the only market certainty, and it puts pressure on corporate budgets. To ensure the marketing organization's value is recognized (and rewarded with a larger budget share), the CMO must be able to talk benefits in business terms (short- and long-term revenue).
Consider investing in the finance and marketing relationship by embedding marketing staff with the finance department and vice versa. It helps ensure that we are all speaking the same language and we understand the expectations we have of each other.
Hopefully, this will be a useful guide to help in some small way to navigate the waters of 2024. Don't miss the GenAI boat, but bear in mind it's not the only trend in town. Trends evolve, so keep your head on a swivel for new developments, and best of luck in the coming year.

title: Council Post: How To Use AI To Help Your Business
text:
Camilo Concha is the Founder & CEO of LendingUSA, a point-of-sale fintech solution to help finance important moments in life.
As everyone knows, AI, or artificial intelligence, is making more of an impact in our world today than ever before. From the financial sector to the automotive industry to healthcare to language models like ChatGPT and beyond, it seems that everywhere you look, you can see evidence of AI advancements. The business world is no exception. There are a multitude of ways in which business owners are taking advantage of AI advancements in order to strengthen their businesses. If you use AI the right way, your business can benefit significantly.
The Numerous Advantages Of Using AI
At the root of why utilizing AI is so advantageous to businesses is the increased efficiency. There are many repetitive tasks and processes that all businesses must do. Examples of such tasks include data entry, employee onboarding, all things billing and payroll, quality control and customer feedback—just to name a few. With AI-powered software, time-consuming tasks like these can be automated so employees can spend more time on other tasks, thus making them more efficient with their time. It also reduces the impact of human error, potentially leading to fewer mistakes that can snowball into big issues for a business.
Another significant sector of most businesses in which AI can be very helpful is customer experience. AI-powered chatbots or personal assistants can make recommendations to customers based on their needs, providing personalized customer interactions and leading to greater customer satisfaction and loyalty. Also, when customers give feedback, AI can quickly analyze said feedback, helping businesses retain customers and increase customer lifetime value. Utilizing AI for interacting with customers also allows businesses to be able to offer support 24/7 and with quick response times around the clock—something that even the best-staffed customer support team of humans can’t do.
Speaking of customers, another use for AI in a business is predictive analysis. Not only can this technology predict customer behavior, it can often predict future market trends. AI can analyze great quantities of data in an extremely short amount of time. This quick analysis provides invaluable insights into trends in the current and future markets. This knowledge is significant and helps in inventory management, pricing strategies and overall business planning.
In a similar vein, not only is data analysis beneficial when it comes to predictions and planning, but it can positively impact many other areas of business. Overall, it helps business owners make informed, evidence-based decisions about strategies, product development and more. For example, businesses must track key performance indicators and metrics to monitor and optimize performance. That way, they can see what they’re doing right or wrong as well as what benchmarks should be set. Similarly, AI can analyze employee data, which can help business leaders identify problems, training needs and, overall, how to optimize workforce management.
Quality control is another area of business in which AI-analyzed data is immensely helpful. Defects or issues in products or processes can be found quickly, improving quality control. In cases of fraud, anomalies or other errors can also be detected quickly, which allows for timely corrective actions as well as fraud prevention. When it comes to compliance, AI can assist with regulatory requirements and reporting obligations.
How To Take Advantage Of AI
The key to using AI for increased efficiency, improving the customer experience, data analysis and any other task is finding and choosing the right AI tool for your need(s). The first step to doing so is to outline both your business objectives and what you want to achieve with AI. Identify the problems you want to address or specific tasks and processes you want simplified with AI. Next, determine your budget. While there are some free AI tools available, typically, they require an initial purchase or subscription. Depending on the type of AI, it could also require training or ongoing maintenance that costs money.
Once your AI needs and budgets have been determined, research AI tools that align with your business objectives. When compiling your list of potential tools, consider factors such as:
• Industry-specific features.
• Ease of use and user interface.
• Customizability.
• Compatibility and integration.
• Vendor reputation.
• Data security and compliance.
Be sure to read reviews or case studies from other people/businesses who have used the AI tools you’re interested in so you can have a real-world example of how people are using these tools, the success they’re seeing, and any limitations or issues they’ve discovered using the tool.
If reviews are favorable, the next step is to request a demo or trial period. Use these to test the tool’s performance, usability and suitability for your business. You could consider conducting a small-scale test of the tool before fully implementing it and integrating it into your business; this way, you won’t waste time fully implementing a tool that you soon realize doesn’t work for your business.
If you run into questions during your trial period, consider consulting with an AI expert who can provide guidance. Once you decide to purchase the tool and fully implement it into your business, don’t forget to continuously monitor the tool’s performance. Measure its impact on your business and calculate the return on investment to ensure it’s worth continuing to pay for and use.
AI: The Future Of Business Practices
The transformative power of artificial intelligence continues to alter many aspects of our lives. In the business world, it is making a clear impact across industries. As advancements in AI technology are made every day, the integration of AI tools into businesses is becoming more than an option.
To stay competitive, businesses must adapt and embrace what AI can do for them. By leveraging the right AI tools, businesses can capitalize on the myriad business practices that are improved and made easier with AI. By embracing these tools, they can not only thrive but potentially be positioned at the forefront of innovation and sustainable growth.

title: Council Post: Bullish But Cautionary: A Balanced Way To Approach The Impact Of AI
text:
President & CEO of BBB National Programs, a nonprofit organization dedicated to fostering a more accountable, trustworthy marketplace.
The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kristalina Georgieva, is bullish on the potential of artificial intelligence (AI), but cautionary, too.
In a blog post timed to coincide with last month’s World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Georgieva wrote that the technology could “jumpstart productivity, boost global growth and raise incomes” but equally could “replace jobs and deepen inequality.” “The AI era is upon us,” wrote Georgieva, “and it is still within our power to ensure it brings prosperity for all.”
Business and nonprofit leaders in the U.S. may not feel so weighty a responsibility in assessing the global impact of AI, but we must realize AI’s power to impact our organizations, our local economies, our sectors and our nation.
Last spring, four key federal government agencies, among them the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau, released a joint statement outlining a commitment to enforce their respective laws and regulations when it comes to AI. More recently, following the Biden Administration’s Executive Order on AI, the Office of Management and Budget issued a directive that will drive government standards as a user and purchaser of AI products.
The proper use of AI is a serious matter and there are several steps for us to take, the first being education, assessment, policy development, governance and process for ourselves and our teams. While that may seem overwhelming, there are plenty of resources available.
Take recruiting and hiring, for example. You may not realize it, but AI is likely involved in your recruiting and hiring process, either overtly through your use of various AI tools for sorting candidates or indirectly through AI’s role in “feeding” newly posted career opportunities to job seekers. Six months ago, I wrote about our project to develop principles and protocols for the use of AI in recruiting and hiring, and today those principles and protocols are more necessary than ever.
A new year also brings about new budgets and financial forecasts. Your organization is probably using an enterprise software system for your budgeting and forecasting and that system likely employs machine learning/AI in its data analysis. Here again, there is an opportunity to not replace members of your finance team but to embrace AI and enable them to produce more accurate, efficient and realistic financial predictions.
In these areas, there is more opportunity than challenge, which should lead to more hope than fear.
But what about the actual product or service that you offer to your customers and stakeholders? And how about the supply chain that enables you to develop and present those products and services?
AI in product development does not have to be mysterious. If your organization has been conducting market research to learn what current or potential customers might want, AI can augment that process, making it “smarter” and allowing your product development leaders to layer their experience and insights on top of a richer recipe of data and analytics.
Your supply chain can also benefit from AI. After all, supply chains improve when they are measured carefully, analyzed deeply and adjusted accordingly. Your process of measurement has probably included AI for years and you either did not know it or did not see a need to think about it. Deep analysis has also benefited greatly from AI injections and, while you probably knew that instinctually, you probably also have not spent much time wrestling with how to maximize the impact of AI.
Beyond the four walls of your own business or nonprofit organization, there are other aspects of AI that you should consider in the context of competitors, peers and customers. Be truthful in your claims about your use of and your commitments to AI and keep a watchful eye on the AI claims and commitments of your competitors as well.
Government agencies are taking steps to ensure that the use of AI follows the law and current regulatory frameworks. Congress has been examining what new laws—or changes to existing laws—need to be made to provide the right level of AI governance while not hampering U.S.-led innovation.
As a December 2023 report from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) stated, "The FTC will continue to closely monitor and scan the developments of these products, services, and tools. As the generative AI industry continues to develop, the FTC will remain vigilant and ready to use the full panoply of its law enforcement and policy tools to foster fair competition, protect consumers, and help ensure that the public benefits from this transformative technology."
This vigilance applies in several different contexts. At BBB National Programs, we are focusing on, among others, the FTC’s enforcement work in misleading advertising by AI, organizational privacy commitments and copyright issues.
We are also looking closely at recent developments in litigation surrounding AI software and alleged unconscious bias and AI and consumer finance products.
Until ChatGPT burst onto the scene, the concept of generative AI seemed on the business horizon and less relevant to many. But now the “transformative technology” of generative AI is here to stay, and it is incumbent for every business and nonprofit leader to assess what it may mean for every aspect of an organization’s operations. It is not just a “back-office” concern; even your frontline workers will likely have to become AI-savvy and AI-co-dependent.
The IMF’s leader, Kristalina Georgieva, is bullish on AI, and you should be, too. She is also cautionary about AI, and you should be as well. There is a balance to be struck and, as business and nonprofit leaders, it is within our power to harness the power of AI for good in our organizations.

title: Council Post: Edge-Of-Network Computing And AI: How AI May Fill Gaps In 5G Tech
text:
Founder of Projetech, Inc.
The automotive industry has experienced rapid advancements due to the integration of edge computing and artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years. As vehicles continue developing self-driving capabilities, these technologies have become increasingly critical for effective decision-making and real-time reactions.
Edge computing processes data and commands locally within a vehicle's systems, improving road safety and transportation efficiency. Combined with 5G, it enables real-time communication between vehicles and infrastructure, reducing latency and allowing autonomous vehicles to respond faster. AI algorithms enable cars to interpret visual data and make human-like driving decisions.
Edge computing and AI are transforming vehicles into true self-driving machines, filling any gaps in low-latency 5G tech and enabling companies to pioneer advanced autonomy.
The Evolution Of Edge Computing And AI Integration
Autonomous vehicles have seen a major shift in computing from centralized servers to decentralized edge devices. This evolution in edge computing has reduced latency, enabling vehicles to interpret sensor data and react to changing road conditions in real time.
By leveraging decentralized nodes and real-time analytics, autonomous vehicles can process visual data, detect obstacles, adjust to unexpected events and make critical driving decisions without any delay, paving the way for fully autonomous cars.
Tesla's thorough collection of real-world driving data provides a unique advantage, allowing them to refine their AI algorithms for autonomous driving. As more drivers gain access to Tesla's Full Self-Driving (FSD) beta software, the software's impressive results in real-world driving conditions become more apparent. The vast amount of visual data collected during these drives aids in the learning process of Tesla's AI, improving its reliability and effectiveness in real-world conditions.
Impact On Industries And Predictive Maintenance
The application of edge computing and AI is revolutionizing the maintenance and reliability sectors across industries. Intelligent sensors and devices can now collect data on temperature, vibration, stress levels and other metrics in real time at the edge. This enables incredibly effective predictive maintenance workflows.
Rather than relying on scheduled maintenance or standard inspections, edge technologies allow for intelligent monitoring of equipment conditions. Potential problems and failures can be predicted before they occur based on data patterns and analytics, preventing costly unplanned downtime and enhancing proactive maintenance capabilities.
Moving condition monitoring and predictive analytics to the edge provides instantaneous insights compared to centralized cloud computing. Industries are rapidly adopting these intelligent systems to achieve new levels of efficiency and reliability. The technology landscape will continue to evolve as more devices operate at the edge and share data insights in real time.
A Future Of Autonomous Vehicles
While there are still challenges to overcome in autonomous vehicles, the future is promising. Autonomous driving could generate between $300 billion and $400 billion in the passenger car market by 2035. Plus, it's predicted that there will be over 33 million driverless vehicles on the road by 2040.
Automakers are taking different approaches to developing autonomous vehicle technology. For example, Tesla is focusing on vision-based systems powered by AI, while General Motors and its subsidiary Cruise are emphasizing lidar sensors along with cameras and radar.
Ford and Volkswagen are collaborating on self-driving cars that combine lidar, radar and cameras with detailed road maps. Waymo, the self-driving unit of Google's parent company, Alphabet, has been testing autonomous minivans with a diverse sensor suite of vision, lidar and radar hardware.
In addition to sensor technology, computing power is crucial for autonomous driving. Automakers like Mercedes and Volvo are partnering with chipmaker Nvidia to utilize their powerful Drive platform, which is designed specifically for self-driving cars.
It's clear the automotive industry is vigorously pursuing self-driving technologies through various innovations. As companies continue innovating, the dream of fully driverless cars is getting closer to reality.
Broader Implications Of AI And Edge Computing
The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotics have far-reaching implications beyond the automotive industry. As autonomous systems powered by AI face more complex real-world variables, the applications of these technologies will transform various sectors.
AI and robotics will integrate deeper into manufacturing, replacing or augmenting human workers to optimize efficiency and output. Intelligent robotic systems can operate tirelessly on assembly lines with precision and consistency. This transformation will lead to higher productivity and economic growth.
The capabilities of AI and machine learning will also enable transformative changes in sectors like healthcare, agriculture, financial services and more. AI diagnostic tools can analyze medical scans and data to support doctors in making quick and accurate diagnoses. Farming equipment and robots can use computer vision, GPS and AI to automate planting, watering and harvesting with minimal human intervention. Fintech applications of AI include algorithmic trading, personalized banking through chatbots and detecting fraud by analyzing patterns.
As edge computing brings increased processing power to devices, combined with rapid improvements in AI, the potential applications are endless.
The Road Ahead: Opportunities And Challenges
According to Gartner, by 2025, 75% of all enterprise data will be processed at the edge, up from just 10% in 2018. This highlights the potential for edge computing to foster unprecedented change.
The future of autonomous vehicles holds tremendous promise, though the path ahead still contains challenges. There have been impressive strides with the FSD beta, demonstrating capabilities like automatic lane changes, navigating complex intersections and detecting traffic lights and stop signs. However, we have yet to achieve full vehicle autonomy in all conditions.
Industry experts vary in their predictions for when fully autonomous cars will be commonplace. However, most agree we will see a gradual progression, with autonomous capabilities increasing over time. This includes more comprehensive implementation of driver assistance features, continued phased testing of self-driving systems and regulatory approval expansion.
Through ongoing research, refined software, accumulated driving data and rigorous real-world validation, the promise of safe autonomous transportation for all could become a reality.
As this technology advances, we can expect even more seamless integration of intelligent edge devices and AI assistants into our lives. With diligent testing and responsible deployment, autonomous technologies supported by edge computing have the potential to augment human capabilities profoundly and transcend current limitations.

title: Council Post: Using Secure Inference To Protect Digital Whispers In AI Conversations
text:
Moran Zavdi is the founder of Nucleon Cyber, which provides actionable, proactive cyber threat intelligence for organizations.
Imagine you're telling a secret to a friend. This might be seeking advice on a personal matter or professional help. Most of the time, you expect this conversation to remain private and away from prying ears. Unsurprisingly, many of us expect the same when it comes to chatting with online AI bots and services.
Today, artificial intelligence is used in many places, but have you stopped to think if your conversations and information are really secured from access by others? Whether using ChatGPT or disclosing health information to a medical app, there are many real-life use cases where we use AI without a second thought. These interactions involve sharing different types of information, both personal and professional. In most cases, we don't want other people to access it.
Think of it like a digital whisper—we divulge certain details to AI services with the expectation that it remains a secret. But as AI is an evolving technology, it's worth taking the time to explore how we can ensure the privacy of these digital whispers.
There are several ways to protect data, and there are many layers of data to protect. In this article, we discuss the concept of secure inference, a technology that can play a crucial role in protecting this data.
Understanding The Inference Process
Have you ever wondered how your chatbots come up with answers to your questions or how your streaming service recommends the perfect show you never knew existed? The secret lies in a special place within the AI system known as inference. Let's examine how it works.
Step 1: Gaining Knowledge
Imagine a big library full of books. This is the AI's training ground, and it's learning by taking in all of the information in those books. But beyond the information in the text itself, the data the AI uses to learn can be almost anything. Whether it's related to words, images or code, it all becomes fuel for its internal knowledge engine.
Step 2: Your Query
To respond, the AI needs to be asked a question. This might be something such as "What's the best restaurant for a romantic date?" or "Should I invest in this stock?" This query is your whisper, and this is where the inference process begins.
Step 3: The Whispering Oracle
Deep within the AI's circuits, billions of neurons fire, tracing connections through its accumulated knowledge. It sifts through mountains of data, whispers possibilities to itself and finally arrives at an answer.
Step 4: The Unveiling
The AI's response emerges, tailored to your needs. This might be a restaurant recommendation or a stock analysis.
But there's a caveat to this picture. Imagine a mischievous imp lurking in the shadows, eager to eavesdrop on your whispers to the AI or peek at its replies. This, unfortunately, is the reality today, where hackers lurk. Your confidential inquiry or the AI's insightful answer could become exposed, turning your private whispers into unwanted shouts.
This is where secure inference steps in, acting as a digital bodyguard for your AI interactions. It helps ensure that only authorized ears hear your whispers and the AI's replies.
Securing The Whispers
Secure inference aims to add a layer of protection to confidential conversations with AI models. Think of it as a secure communication channel, ensuring only authorized parties can hear your whispers and the model's reply.
Some techniques used to achieve this are:
Homomorphic Encryption
Homomorphic encryption is sort of like a special lock on a safe that lets you perform calculations on the contents inside the safe without needing to unlock it. Just like how the lock allows manipulation of the items inside without direct access, homomorphic encryption enables computations on encrypted data, preserving its confidentiality until the results are decrypted.
When considering homomorphic encryption, it's important to analyze your organization's specific needs. This entails first assessing whether this approach aligns with specific security requirements. Then, be sure to choose homomorphic encryption libraries and tools that align with your organization's technical stack and the expertise of the IT team.
Secure Multi-Party Computation
Secure multi-party computation (SMPC) is more akin to multiple friends whispering secrets to each other, able to share their unique knowledge without revealing any of the secrets they've come to discover from individual friends. In this way, several parties contribute data and perform computations without revealing their individual inputs, allowing them to perform collaborative AI analysis without compromising privacy.
When looking to effectively implement SMPC, select the SMPC protocol appropriate to the specific use case concerning data size, computation complexity and the number of parties involved. It's critical to make sure it's compliant with related data privacy regulations such as GDPR, CCPA or HIPAA.
Differential Privacy
Think of this as adding a touch of static to a radio transmission to mask the original message. Differential privacy (DP) adds controlled noise to your data during training, protecting individual privacy while still allowing the model to learn from collective information.
The fundamental challenge in DP is balancing privacy protection with the utility of the data. Adding noise to data can reduce its accuracy. It's also important to note that the added noise can impact certain types of data analysis more than others. Understanding this impact is essential for interpreting results correctly.
Beyond Privacy
Secure inference goes beyond just protecting these digital whispers. For businesses, this could mean a secure analysis of sensitive customer data for better products and services without privacy concerns. For healthcare, it might better ensure confidential medical diagnosis and treatment recommendations based on patient data without compromising privacy. In finance, this can safeguard financial transactions and fraud detection while keeping individual financial information secure.
As we continue to integrate AI more deeply into our daily lives, the responsibility to guard our communications grows. Before trusting your personal or professional secrets to an AI service, dive into their privacy policies and security measures. Question whether advanced protections like homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation or differential privacy are being used. Make informed decisions by choosing services that not only claim to protect your data but also demonstrate it through transparent, robust and verifiable privacy practices. In the digital age, your privacy is as valuable as the information you share. Be the guardian of your digital whispers.

title: Council Post: Why Every Business Needs Its Own GPT
text:
CEO and cofounder of Glean.
Consumers are adopting generative AI faster than any technology in recent memory. OpenAI, Microsoft and Google are embedding it into the tools and platforms used a billion times daily by people around the world.
And given the potential of a tool like generative AI for the workplace, businesses are chasing close behind in trying to figure out how to incorporate a version of ChatGPT into their workflows. Generative AI is already used by 37% of marketers, 35% of technology teams and 30% of consultants, according to a Statista study from last December.
Why? Open generative AI models can seemingly perform a stunning variety of knowledge tasks. People are using it to write and check software code, draft marketing campaigns or press releases and produce HR policy documents and onboarding materials. Some are looking to use it to accelerate search and knowledge discovery across businesses of any size like nothing we’ve ever seen before.
As someone who has spent most of their career working with AI, especially as applied to search, I have to say—hang on a minute. This speed of adoption is risky. Large language models (LLM) like ChatGPT do represent an enormous improvement in coherency (the ability of AI to produce sense-making answers), but open models don’t deliver any value if they can’t deliver their answers in a business context. One accidental error or confidential leak can trigger serious privacy and security violations.
Before we can rely on LLMs in the enterprise, the technology has to deliver on three major requirements: accuracy, trust and permissions.
Accuracy
An off-the-shelf model like ChatGPT 4 or Bard can produce wrong answers so confidently that a non-subject-matter-expert would have a devilish time identifying the flaw. This renders open-model generative AI inconsistent at best and disastrous at worst. A study from April 2023 audited four popular generative search engines and found that, on average, only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations, and only 74.5% of citations supported their associated sentence. They’re right—these results are “concerningly low for systems that may serve as a primary tool for information-seeking users.”
The business setting requires responses that are correct in their nuance, not just understandable and directionally correct. To understand precisely which information to surface, an enterprise AI has to understand an organization's intricacies, policies, language, and how teams and individuals collaborate, along with many other factors. Getting rid of “creative errors” requires an enterprise LLM to be trained on a specific domain (law, insurance, oil & gas) or company knowledge graph, especially for semantic tasks like search.
Knowledge domains are like Russian nesting dolls: Within each domain, there are sub-domains, each with its language. Some tasks require more domain knowledge than others. For example, for named entity recognition (plucking out proper names), a model trained in the English language will be good (because the domain is not super important).
But, an LLM trained in my company’s specific knowledge graph would know that a search for Scholastic should return information about our data retrieval and scoring model, also called Scholastic. If you were to type questions about Scholastic into ChatGPT 4, you’d likely get responses about curriculum, education or the children’s book publishing company. Similarly, Bloomberg’s GPT, trained on 50 billion parameters from its financial data, significantly outperforms open models on natural language processing in the financial services domain.
Trust
There are critical aspects of trust businesses need to have in place before they can reliably use generative AI in the enterprise. For starters, the results must be human-interpretable. Everyone in an organization has to know how the model generates the answers it provides.
Transparency is another critical contributor to trust. The provenance of any generated answer should be clear and explicit: creator, date, the context of its creation, how it adheres to data governance policies and, ideally, its relationship to other materials and source files. Humans have to be in the loop. They need tools like free-form text fields to alert admins and up- or down-voting to flag inaccuracies to feel like they can trust the machine.
Permissions
No company would (or should) set loose an open-model LLM on its company’s information without first guaranteeing its users only see answers they’re allowed to see. Enterprise LLMs can and must adhere to a company’s privacy rules and data governance policies, just as any enterprise application would. However, generative AI changes the nature of the data governance problem.
Company-specific LLMs can reduce the chance of information leakage because they’ve already modeled the company’s unique language. A system built on words in that domain or restricted to that company’s knowledge will better understand if and when certain people have access to that information. It can better answer questions like, “Is the information we’re generating for you specific to the documents you can access?” (This problem won’t disappear as long as concepts like information and documents remain blurry.)
Generative AI will be a critical force multiplier for knowledge workers. Still, we must ensure the models that businesses depend on for critical knowledge discovery are based on a stable, secure and trusted foundation. We’re far from taking our hands off the wheel; even the most trusted knowledge models need human oversight. But the generated truth is out there.

title: 5 ChatGPT Prompts To Optimize Your Sales Funnel (and Boost Conversion)
text:
If there’s one thing to get right in your business, it’s your sales funnel. Without one that stands up to testing, any marketing efforts will be fleeting and shallow. It’s not enough to grab attention, you have to keep it. You have to get people hooked on your message, spending their time with your content, and nurtured through your flow ready to buy. Sort this out as a matter of priority.
ChatGPT can optimize your sales funnel with the right prompts. I asked five AI and prompting specialists for their top tips on how entrepreneurs can set up for success. Copy, paste and edit the square brackets in ChatGPT, and address each element of your funnel one by one, testing as you go along.
Boost conversion with ChatGPT: improve every stage of your funnel
Visualize each stage
Before you optimize your sales funnel, you need to know what every stage comprises. Without that, you’re stuck before you begin. Dan Linden, co-founder of Chief AI Officer swears by this method. “For me it’s most helpful to visualize content for each stage of the funnel. Even if someone knows what a funnel is, most can’t match the content type to the particular stage.” He gets this right with the following prompt, to plan every aspect of content based on these results.
“Generate customized content ideas for each stage of the sales funnel, based on the following business details: [describe your business]. Carefully considering my goal, which is [describe your main business objective], create three content ideas for each of the following stages of the sales funnel: Awareness, interest, consideration, intent, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase. For each stage, list the ideas in a chart format, ensuring a step-by-step approach for clear and actionable strategies.”
Understand your audience
Once you know your customer inside-out, you can provide the solution to solve their problems. Darby Rollins, founder and CEO of Gen AI University, said awareness is key, because “how can your business solve a problem if your customers don’t know who you are?” Even if they do, “is your messaging speaking to them or are you missing the mark?” Rollins recommends you use AI for market research, to better understand your target audience and create content that speaks to them where they are at from awareness to conversion. To do this, fill in the blanks with information about your business and run the following prompt.
“As a skilled marketer and customer researcher, your role is to delve into the psychology that influences buying decisions for [product/service] with the goal of [descrbe your business goal]. Start by identifying the main market segments relevant to [product/service]. One at a time, analyze each segment to understand its unique characteristics. Following this, develop a core content brief tailored to buyers within each segment, specifically for [product/service] in the [niche]. This involves a detailed examination of the audience to grasp their challenges, interests, and behaviors, focusing on their geographic location, demographic details (job roles, industry, age, income, etc.), psychographic traits (needs, wants, desires, and behaviors), and pain points. Your analysis should uncover the psychological and social factors that drive this market segment, enabling you to create content that resonates on a deep emotional level, without directly mentioning my product or company. Instead, focus on the human aspects we are researching. Articulate these insights into bullet points, each starting with a bolded section name for clarity, providing a comprehensive view into the target audience's mindset and its connection to my product within my niche of [your niche].”
Improve your headlines
Headlines go right at the top of any website or landing page, and a good one can make you sales more than anything else people read. It’s a solid bottom-of-the-funnel exercise to nail from the start. Kyle Balmer, founder of the AI Business Breakthrough Academy, said that not only are headlines “the first and most important textual element on any page,” but “they provide the basic hook that leads a visitor to read the rest of the page. Without a good headline the rest of the page is unimportant.” He said that A/B testing a variety of headlines is a top priority task, and uses this prompt in ChatGPT to do exactly that.
“As a copywriter specializing in website sales pages, your task is to craft 10 potential headlines for my business, [describe your business], highlighting its primary benefits [benefits] to your specified audience [provide audience details]. The objective is to create short, clear, and impactful headlines that encourage visitors to continue exploring the page. Ensure your headlines are varied, incorporating elements such as numbers for specificity, humor to engage, surprising statements to captivate, and negative framing to address potential concerns or reverse psychology tactics. This approach aims to cover a broad range of strategies to attract and retain the attention of your audience, ultimately guiding them through the sales funnel.”
Optimize for desire
Visualization is a powerful tool in an entrepreneur’s toolbox. Switching your potential customer’s brain to a visionary channel will mean your business becomes part of their fantasy, leading them ever closer to signing up. Isabella Bedoya, founder of MarketingPros.ai, said it’s important to optimize the “desire” stage of your sales funnel, which is right in the middle. Her powerful tactic is to “add a visualization component that engages the potential customer by creating a mental image of the impact that the product or service can have on their lives.” Do this to “form an emotional connection with your potential buyer, shifting interest into desire, and increasing likelihood of conversions.” Insert this ChatGPT-crafted paragraph onto your website. Use this ChatGPT prompt to help you on your way.
“As an award-winning sales copywriter skilled in human behavior and buyer's psychology, you're tasked with creating a ‘desire’ section for my [product/service]. Incorporate these key details: [describe your product/service], the problems it solves [describe these], and my target audience [describe target audience]. Craft a narrative that encapsulates the emotional and tangible benefits of my offering, leading to a compelling piece that emphasizes the unique value proposition and how it addresses the needs and desires of the target audience. Your narrative should seamlessly blend the desired feeling of achievement, the allure for the type of clients it attracts, the adjective that best describes the desired outcome, and how it enriches relationships with loved ones or clients, making them feel a specific emotion. This should be creatively integrated into a concise yet powerful section that leverages the AIDA marketing framework to spark interest, build desire, and motivate action. Only provide me with 150 words or fewer for the desire stage.”
Address retention
It’s no good setting up a perfect funnel, optimizing your sales pages and generating high levels of desire if you can’t follow through on your promise. Don’t forget retention is part of the complete sales cycle. Heather Murray, founder of AI for Non-Techies, said “this stage of the sales funnel often needs attention.” But she knows it’s key. “Retain clients by understanding what they think of you and fixing any issues.” Murray put forward this prompt, so you can “pull together a structured client questionnaire to dig into all the important factors of service quality.”
“As an expert in client retention and satisfaction, you are tasked with designing a client satisfaction survey for my business that sells [product/service] to [audience]. Our clients need help with [problem], and we provide them with [solution]. Your survey should be grounded in the SERVQUAL model by Parasuraman et al., focusing on its five dimensions: tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy. The questions you craft should specifically cater to my [product/service] and audience, aiming to elicit responses that offer actionable insights to enhance our client relationships and boost retention. Make sure the survey questions are relevant and thought-provoking, covering: (1) Tangibles: Appearance of physical facilities, equipment, personnel, and communication materials. (2) Reliability: Ability to perform the promised service dependably and accurately. (3) Responsiveness: Willingness to help customers and provide prompt service. (4) Assurance: Knowledge and courtesy of employees and their ability to inspire trust and confidence. (5) Empathy: Caring, individualized attention the firm provides its customers. The survey should be concise enough to be completed within 15 minutes when sent via email, ensuring a high response rate while gathering comprehensive feedback to inform improvements in our client service strategy.”
Optimize your sales funnel: ChatGPT prompts for significant improvements
Unpack your funnel and build it back together with the help of these five prompts from five AI professionals that know their stuff. Visualize content at every stage before you go ahead, understand your audience and walk in their shoes, and improve your headlines to grab attention. Optimize for desire to spark an emotional connection and address retention so you keep everyone you convert. Make significant improvements with these simple tips.

title: 2024: A Spatial Computing Odyssey Charts A Course To A Metaverse
text:
Introducing new experiences between screens and physical spaces, spatial computing accelerates Web3D and reinvigorates the metaverse
Generative AI may have dominated headlines since November 2022, but 2024 will be the year when spatial computing shares the spotlight. Apple’s highly anticipated Vision Pro is now shipping, with its pre-order stock selling out in 18 minutes. While not indicative of its ultimate success, it offers a glimpse into the market’s appetite to explore new digital experiences. Meta, Magic Leap, Sony, and other hardware leaders are also setting the course for new augmented and virtual reality applications. They’re not only paving the way for extended reality and spatial computing, but also changing the way we connect, interact, consume, and create. They’re also setting the stage for the next era of computing and work.
As the chapter of spatial computing unfolds, it raises the question: Is this a new future of “Web3D”? And will it replace the metaverse?
Whatever Happened To The Metaverse?
As a popular term, “metaverse” practically vanished overnight, with some experts wondering whether the concept or trend was dead. These days, it’s even being referred to as the “M” word. But rumors of the metaverse’s demise may have been greatly exaggerated.
Meta’s VP of Metaverse, Vishal Shah, an influential leader in this next era of computing, believes the hype, not the idea, of the metaverse is dead. In an interview with Fortune, Shaw referred to Gartner’s Hype Cycle, saying “"…we didn't invest for the hype, we have been investing in the space for years.”
You can say that the metaverse is currently traversing through the “Trough of Disillusionment,” the phase that sits between the “Peak of Inflated Expectations” and the “Slope of Enlightenment.” This is a key phase in the evolution of any emergent technology when leaders must see beyond the initial enthusiasm to develop pragmatic and innovative applications that prove viability and scale adoption.
Spatial Computing Is A Platform For Immersive Experiences
The promise of a metaverse will be fulfilled by the visionaries and supporting technologies who give it meaning over the coming decade. Whether it moves beyond the “Trough of Disillusionment” is dependent on the appeal, viability, and adoption of emerging applications and use cases. Spatial computing doesn’t replace the idea of a metaverse. It may enable it.
Apple describes its new visionOS platform as “an infinite canvas for apps that scales beyond the boundaries of a traditional display and introduces a fully three-dimensional user interface controlled by the most natural and intuitive inputs possible — a user’s eyes, hands, and voice.” In this case, it helps to think of spatial computing as a bridge toward a 3-D immersive web, connected by augmented and virtual applications and worlds.
CEO Tim Cook said that he believes “augmented reality is a profound technology.” The gateway to an immersive digital future starts with hybrid experiences. At its launch event, Apple described the Vision Pro as “a revolutionary spatial computer that seamlessly blends digital content with the physical world.”
To Apple, a natural next step in its evolution is to bring the physical and digital world to life in a way that eventually breaks us free from the limitations of computers, traditional entertainment centers, and phones to create new dimensions and interaction layers with the world around us. Apple’s Vision Pro is part of a larger trend accelerating, and shifting, our trajectory toward a new web. And eventually, a true metaverse will mean breaking away from all devices, computers or phones or headsets.
The Space Between Spatial Computing And A Metaverse
The truth is that no one knows how exactly the metaverse will evolve, but we will see progress toward something quite literally in and out of this world. For example, in late 2023, Mark Zuckerberg joined podcast host and computer scientist Lex Fridman surprises audiences by appearing as photorealistic avatars powered by Meta’s own technology. It was an incredible demonstration of real-time interaction, in a virtual space, where Zuckerberg and Fridman could see each other as if they were in the same room together. Meta’s photorealistic avatars were voiced by spatial audio to create a live sensation while also the ability to visually express emotions, naturally, took the words “uncanny valley” out of the equation.
But here’s something to note. Fridman opened the show by saying that the conversation was taking place inside the metaverse. Perhaps its origin story and early definitions may no longer represent what the term “metaverse” means today. In some circles, it’s evolved, for better or worse, to mean “virtual world.” In fact, Zuckerberg described the Metaverse as a place, unlike your phone or computer, where you can do things together with other people in a shared space.
“I think we’re moving towards a world where we’re going to have something that looks like normal glasses, where you can see the physical world, but you’ll also see holograms,” Zuckerberg explained. “And in that world, I think that there are going to be, not too far off, maybe by the end of this decade, we’ll be living in a world where there are as many holograms when you walk into a room as there are physical objects.”
Spatial computing may pave the way toward this augmented reality. A recent post on X by Andrew Schwartz, Director of Metaverse Engineering at Nike, shared his view, which describes a bridge between spatial computing and a metaverse.
“If the organizing principle of the internet is that information wants to be shared, and the organizing principle of the metaverse is that information wants to be experienced, spatial computing brings together the tools necessary to create those experiences,” he observed.
Exploring The Future Of Business Through A Spatial Lens
The question for executives is to look beyond the hype, to work alongside innovators, to collaborate toward the next chapter of computing and the web itself. Forward-thinking leaders are already making investments to not miss opportunities to connect with communities, gain literacy and experience, and understand new ways to cultivate new brand, services, and business opportunities. Most recently, Ralph Lauren CEO Patrice Louvet singled out a metaverse and sustainability as the two key investment areas for attracting Gen Z.
“We are investing in the metaverse,” Louvet told Bloomberg. “We want to be where our consumer is. "That's where they want to engage with brands like us.”
There are already several promising use cases that follow in the footsteps of Ralph Lauren to develop promising virtual worlds and experiences. Threekit is helping brands create 3D and augmented reality assets to unlock immersive shopping experiences called “visual commerce.” Obsess is helping retailers convert traditional 2D ecommerce sites into fully immersive 3D stores that invites shoppers to roam shopping environments virtually. Furniture retailer Serendipity created a shopping portal on a beach in Florida where consumers could “virtually” walk through a pop-up showroom and then return to the beach when ready. Deloitte envisions new dimensions for enterprise applications as well.
Digital twins can already replicate the performance of real-world assets to test new capabilities and scenarios, identify failure rates, and assess how they interact with other smart devices. With AI and private LLMs, digital twins can also simulate customer and buyer personas and market feedback. Spatial simulation allows businesses to replicate facilities or design new models before breaking ground to assess and optimize performance, choke points and failure rates, and perform against different processes and conditions.
NVIDIA AI and Omniverse uses Generative AI to create collaborative metaverse where virtual recreations of vehicle prototypes, interiors, roads and highways, and real-life scenarios for autonomous test drives help teams accelerate design, safety, and time to market. NVIDIA and Omniverse use AI to create digital twins of manufacturing plants and distribution centers to design and optimize workflows 24/7 without having to purchase equipment or build facilities. Then synthetic data then can be used to deploy new designs, workflows and also retrain AI models in the real world.
In its research, Deloitte found that 92% of manufacturers are already experimenting with or implementing at least one metaverse-related use case. On average, they are currently running more than six. As Deloitte describes, “The optimal way to interact with these full-scale digital twins is through AR, a medium that can overlay the physical world with a digital layer to create a shared, three-dimensional immersive internet.”
Putting The Spatial Computing To Work
Spatial computing is officially here. Metaverse-like worlds are also already opening doorways to new consumer, business, and enterprise applications and experiences. Some call this next phase Web 3.0. Others call it Web 3D. Whatever we call it, the next web is spatial and immersive, connecting digital and physical spaces and options, and already under construction.
Spatial computing, extended reality, and the metaverse (as defined as an infinitely scalable interoperable world), will radically enhance and reimagine operations, R&D, customer and employee experiences, and ultimately markets. At an individual level, we thought we blurred the line between digital and physical with our smartphones. Most of us haven’t yet seen or experienced anything like an immersive 3-D web. But we’re about to. Whatever this looks like doesn’t just happen. This future materializes because people like you envision, create, and embrace it.
This article was co-authored with Julia Martensen, a futurist and ServiceNow field innovation officer who advises executives on business transformation.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Is Here To Stay: It’s Time To Get On Board Securely
text:
Shreyans Mehta is the co-founder and CTO of Cequence Security, a pioneer of unified API protection.
Generative AI is a term that dominated headlines and conversations overnight. The technology has made its way into every industry with endless use cases. The most common use cases, like code development and content writing, come to mind first, but even platforms like Spotify use it to give better user experiences.
Most seem excited to welcome generative AI with open arms, but many business executives are hesitant to adopt AI-powered tools, citing the endless risks associated with the technology. As a CTO and security practitioner, I understand the concerns, especially from a cybersecurity perspective.
The truth is that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Bard will ultimately simplify our lives by reducing the amount of time we spend on repetitive basic tasks. And no matter your opinion on generative AI, it’s here for the foreseeable future. Business leaders must create the right policies and controls to ensure their organizations use these tools to increase productivity without bringing on additional risks.
The Bright Side Of Generative AI
The power of generative AI is a double-edged sword, holding the promise of progress and the risk of regression, demanding careful stewardship to ensure its beneficial impact on humanity. Threat actors will exploit the same capabilities that the everyday user can access. They'll develop increasingly sophisticated techniques to mimic human interactions, blurring the lines between human and bot activity.
Although generative AI does present some challenges, its potential to simplify and streamline security operations is undeniable. Today’s security operations centers (SOCs) are overwhelmed by constant security alerts, requiring them to discern genuine threats from false positives. Generative AI can significantly reduce this burden by rapidly investigating each alert and providing actionable insights.
Generative AI is poised to transform security testing, particularly for APIs. Currently, this process is highly manual, with developers creating the software and the QA team crafting corresponding tests. Generative AI can automate this process, generating test cases efficiently and consistently, significantly reducing manual effort and ensuring more comprehensive coverage.
Facing The Generative AI Reality
It’s clear that there are plenty of risks associated with generative AI, from being leveraged by threat actors to the risk of it being inaccurate. And it’s understandable why executives from all industries are on the fence about adopting AI. However, business leaders must recognize that generative AI isn't a passing fad but a fundamental shift in the technological landscape.
Rather than avoiding it or refusing to use it, business leaders must learn how to live with it and embrace it. This isn't to say that we must ignore the risks but instead understand them and work toward adopting the right policies and controls to ensure generative AI is used properly within your business.
As business leaders explore the potential of AI tools, they should focus on these critical factors for effective implementation:
1. Prioritize secure data sharing. Organizations must embrace secure data sharing as the cornerstone of a robust and resilient AI-driven future. Although AI undoubtedly represents a remarkable leap in human innovation and potential, its responsible and ethical implementation is paramount. The focus shouldn't be solely on acquiring AI tools but should encompass the responsibility and accountability for secure integration, particularly when enabled through APIs.
2. Get complete visibility into what data generative AI tools are accessing. Data visibility is a crucial piece of the AI puzzle. Business leaders must have complete transparency into what data their generative AI tools access, when and for what purpose. This helps ensure responsible AI usage, minimizes security risks and maximizes the value gleaned from these powerful tools.
3. Assess your posture management to detect oversharing and sharing without authentication. This involves a comprehensive understanding of what data is being shared, how it's being shared (with or without authentication) and the potential consequences of oversharing. Ask yourself: Are you giving users more information than they requested? Is their personal identifiable (PII) or protected health information (PHI) included in the shared data? Do users have appropriate access controls in place, or should access be restricted?
4. Detect the misuse of good credentials by bad actors. This involves distinguishing legitimate access from unauthorized access attempts, even when good credentials are used. Ideally, this detection should occur in real time, without relying on multiple third-party tools, to minimize potential damage and disruption.
Looking Ahead
Every few years, a new technology comes around that makes big waves, making business leaders cautious about adopting the latest and greatest before it's fully understood. It’s easy to look at the negatives, but executives must look at the positives generative AI can bring to their teams across their organizations and even themselves. With the proper controls in place, business leaders can find peace knowing that they've adopted new technology to empower their employees while taking the right steps to prevent risk.
